theme_summary: Five stories, one thread: the systems we rely on are being asked to adapt quickly, while trust, infrastructure, and good judgment still take time.
editorial_note: Every institution seems to be making faster decisions than ever before. Hospitals, governments, markets, and technology companies are all adapting to accelerating change. Today’s edition is not about speed. It is about understanding what happens when the world starts moving faster than the people responsible for guiding it.
five_things: AI spending is becoming an economic story, not just a technology story.
Congress is again testing the limits of presidential war powers.
Markets are watching inflation because it touches mortgages, hiring, and retirement savings.
Hospitals are deciding where AI helps clinicians—and where it gets in the way.
The next scientific breakthroughs may depend as much on infrastructure as invention.

feature.headline: The new AI arms race is about who can afford it.
feature.deck: The next phase of artificial intelligence will be decided not only by smarter models, but by who can pay for the chips, power, and infrastructure required to run them.
paragraphs: Picture a hospital executive looking at two proposals. One promises better care and less paperwork. The other shows the cost of the data-center capacity, cybersecurity, training, and oversight needed to make it work.
That is where the AI conversation is heading. The question is no longer whether these tools are impressive. It is whether institutions can afford to use them responsibly.

For companies, the financial stakes are enormous. For hospitals, the stakes are even more personal. A system that saves clinicians time can improve care. A system that creates confusion can do the opposite.
feature.pull_quote: Technology moves quickly. Trust does not.
feature.why_it_matters: The biggest technology story of the decade may not be the models themselves, but the systems required to support them.
feature.bottom_line: The winners of the AI era will be the organizations that can afford the technology without losing the trust of the people expected to use it.

stories.headline: Congress pushes back on presidential war powers.
stories.body: The argument is not only about one conflict. It is about who gets to decide when the country uses force—and how much power Congress is willing to reclaim.
stories.bottom_line: Constitutional debates become practical very quickly when lives, alliances, and military commitments are at stake.

stories.headline: Wall Street’s new concern: AI is getting expensive.
stories.body: Investors still believe in the technology. They are beginning to ask whether every company can afford the race, and how long it will take for massive spending to become real profit.
stories.bottom_line: Excitement is easy. Earning back the investment is harder.

stories.headline: The grid behind the AI boom.
stories.body: Data centers need enormous amounts of electricity. That turns energy policy into a technology story—and makes old infrastructure newly important.
stories.bottom_line: The future of AI may depend as much on wires, power plants, and permitting as on software.

stories.headline: AI is quietly changing the doctor’s office.
stories.body: Not by replacing physicians, but by changing how they document visits, review information, and identify patterns in patient care.
stories.provider_impact: Good technology should return time to clinicians, support judgment, and fit into the reality of a busy hospital or practice.
stories.patient_impact: The real test is whether innovation leads to safer care, earlier answers, better access, or a better quality of life.
stories.bottom_line: AI will matter in healthcare only if it improves the relationship between patients and clinicians rather than getting in the way of it.

stories.headline: What happens when every decision has to be made faster?
stories.body: Technology speeds up choices. Wisdom does not. That gap may define the next decade.
stories.bottom_line: Moving faster is not the same as moving well.
